kernel.why: The kernel is what sos-ingest is allowed to carry, so nothing here may grow a dependency on a control-plane module. Every other package under internal/ is a control-plane module by default, which is what fences a package added tomorrow before anyone remembers this file exists.

rules.why: sos-ingest is a separate binary so a bad control-plane deploy cannot take SOS with it. An import reaching into control-plane code rebuilds that coupling without changing anything observable: the binary still starts, still answers in under 50 ms, and now ships whenever the control plane does. The list is also the ≤5-direct-dependency half of the §2.5.1 budget.

A library importing a binary inverts the dependency and drags main's flags, signal handling and process lifetime into every consumer. It also makes the binary untestable in isolation, which is the property sos-ingest's own pipeline depends on.

The kernel is shared with sos-ingest. One kernel package importing a control-plane module drags the whole control plane into the sacred binary through the back door, and the allow_only rule above would still pass because the offending import is not written in cmd/sos-ingest.

allow_edges.why: escalation declares the Fanouter interface itself and *notify.Notifier satisfies it — the consumer-defined-interface pattern §2.5.3 asks for. The import carries only the Step/Channel contract types the ladder names.
The surfacing job publishes an access-log disclosure onto the bus, and notify owns the Frame/Priority contract. consent calls no notify behaviour.

rules.why: One control-plane module may not import another; vault importing journey is the canonical example. This is what lets a module be extracted into its own binary in 2029 without a rewrite. Cross-module calls go through a consumer-defined interface or a bus event, and every exception is listed here with its reason.
